stops.name: Herstal, the Pippinid hall on the Meuse (birthplace uncertain: Herstal? Aachen? Quierzy?)
stops.campa: A boy is born to Pepin the Short and Bertrada of the great foot, in one of the Pippinid halls along the Meuse, Herstal by the oldest habit of the family, though the cradle is nowhere fixed and the canon keeps its silence honestly. The Lorsch calendar will one day write the second of April against his name. He is Charles, grandson of the Hammer who broke the Saracens at Poitiers. The Meuse runs grey past the villa; the mayors of the palace already rule kings who do not rule.

stops.name: Basilica of Saint-Denis, Pope Stephen anoints Pepin and his sons
stops.campa: Pope Stephen II, who has crossed the Alps in winter to beg the Frankish sword against the Lombards, rises in the abbey of the martyr Denis and pours the holy oil on Pepin, on Carloman, and on the boy Charles, twelve years old. In one act the papacy and the Franks are wed. The pope binds the Frankish nobles under pain of interdict never again to choose a king sprung from other loins. The boy feels the oil dry on his forehead; the throne of Peter has laid its hand on the house of Pepin forever.
stops.quote: …that they should never presume in time to come to choose a king sprung from the loins of any other line.

stops.name: Saint-Denis, the death of Pepin the Short
stops.campa: Pepin, returning from crushing Aquitaine, is seized by fever at Saintes and carried north to die where he was anointed. On the twenty-fourth of September he gives back his soul at Saint-Denis and is buried, at his own bidding, face down before the threshold for the sins of his father. The realm is divided by Frankish custom between the two sons: Charles the elder takes the outer crescent of the kingdom, Carloman the rich inner lands. The brothers do not love each other. The abbey bells toll a king who made the crown real.

stops.name: Noyon, Charles raised king of the Franks
stops.campa: On the ninth of October, in the cathedral city of Noyon, the magnates lift Charles on the shield of the Franks and set the crown on him, while on the same day at Soissons his brother Carloman is crowned over the other half. Two kings, one realm, one jealousy. Charles is twenty-six, tall, thick-necked, with the large clear eyes Einhard will remember; his voice is thinner than his frame. The oil of Saint-Denis, fourteen years dry, begins its work.

stops.name: Fronsac on the Dordogne, the first war fought alone
stops.campa: Aquitaine rises under old Hunald, and Carloman refuses his brother aid, turning home from Duasdives with his host. Charles goes on alone. He drives to the Dordogne and builds the fortress of Fronsac on its rock above the river, and from there sends envoys to Lupus, duke of the Gascons, demanding the rebel. Lupus, weighing the new king, hands Hunald over with his wife. The first war of the reign ends without a battle lost: the young king has learned that a fort, a demand, and patience can conquer a duchy.

stops.name: Samoussy, the death of Carloman
stops.campa: At the royal villa of Samoussy, on the fourth of December, King Carloman dies of a flux of blood at the nose and mouth, twenty years old. The rivalry that was ripening toward war, over Aquitaine, over the Lombard marriage their mother made and Charles repudiated, dissolves in a night. His widow Gerberga gathers her infant sons and flees, not to her brother-in-law but over the Alps to Desiderius the Lombard, and by that flight fixes the road Charles must one day take. He is buried at Reims. The whole realm hangs loose, waiting for one hand.

stops.name: Corbeny, the whole realm his
stops.campa: Within days the great men of Carloman's kingdom, Wilchar the archbishop, Fulrad the chaplain, counts Warin and Adalhard, ride to Charles at the villa of Corbeny and commend themselves to him, passing over the dead king's sons in their cradles. There is no election, no war: the Franks simply turn, as a field turns to the sun. Charles receives their hands between his and is king of all the Franks. From this winter villa on the Laon road, the single reign begins that will not end for forty-three years.

stops.name: Worms, the assembly decrees the Saxon war
stops.campa: At Worms on the Rhine the first great assembly of the sole reign gathers, and the king proposes war on the Saxons, the pagan neighbor that burns churches on the border and honors trees and springs. Thirty-three years of war are decreed in an afternoon, though no man there knows it. The host is blessed, the standards raised; the Franks march northeast into the woodland where the old gods still hold their courts. Einhard will write that no war was ever longer, crueler, or more full of toil.

stops.name: The Eresburg, the Saxon fortress stormed
stops.campa: The army comes up out of the Diemel valley against the Eresburg, the hill-fortress of the Saxons on its steep table of rock. The Franks take it by storm; the gates are burned, a garrison installed, and a church will stand where the rampart-shrine stood. From its height the king looks north into Saxony: forest to the edge of sight, no roads, no writing, no baptism. Somewhere in that green dark stands the pillar the Saxons say upholds the universe. He gives the order to march to it.

stops.name: The Irminsul, the world-pillar felled
stops.campa: In a sacred grove near the Eresburg stands the Irminsul, the universal column of the pagans, the trunk they say carries the sky. Charles comes to it with axes. For the Saxons this is the ending of the world; for the Franks it is the beginning of Saxony's salvation. The great pillar goes down, the grove is fired, and three days are spent destroying the sanctuary utterly. From under the shrine the Franks lift the treasure of generations, the gold and silver of a whole people's vows, and carry it away in the king's train. The sky, the chroniclers note, does not fall.
stops.quote: He destroyed this idol and carried away the gold and silver which he found there.

stops.name: The camp by the Irminsul, the spring at noon
stops.campa: A great drought lies on the land, and in the place where the Irminsul stood there is no water; the army, laboring at the destruction of the temple, begins to fail with thirst. Then at noon, while the host rests and no man is drawing or digging, water bursts from the ground in a stream: enough for the whole army, poured out by the grace of God in the very footprint of the felled idol. The Franks read the sign plainly: the God of the Christians waters His soldiers where the false pillar stood. The king lets the army drink, then finishes the burning.
stops.quote: Suddenly at noon, through the grace of God, while the army rested and nobody knew what was happening, so much water poured forth in a stream that the whole army had enough.

stops.name: Geneva, the muster for Italy
stops.campa: Pope Hadrian's envoys have come by sea, since the Lombard holds the roads: Desiderius has seized the cities of Peter and demands the pope anoint Carloman's little sons kings of the Franks. Charles offers gold for peace three times; three times the Lombard refuses. So at Geneva, where the Rhone leaves the lake, the Frankish host divides in two: the king will take the Mont Cenis, his uncle Bernard the Great Saint Bernard, the two horns of an army closing on Lombardy. The lake lies flat and bright; beyond it the wall of the Alps, and beyond the wall, Italy.
